## Course Description and Objectives

<!-- Duplicated from index.qmd — keep the two in sync on every edit. -->

In this course, Honors students learn how to turn curiosity into credible, evidence-based insight without requiring a strong background in quantitative methods or computing. Students will learn to identify meaningful gaps in a chosen field, translate those gaps into well-scoped research problems, and formulate research questions that can be answered with data. Through a structured, supported workflow, students learn how to select and justify an appropriate quantitative method approach (description, statistical inference, predictive modeling, and/or causal reasoning) and how to use computational tools and AI to locate sources, operationalize concepts, analyze evidence, verify results, and document decisions responsibly. By the end of the course, students will be enabled to design and defend a rigorous research approach, interpret findings with appropriate uncertainty and limitations, and communicate results effectively in written and oral formats.

**Course Website**: [https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/){target="_blank"}

## Learning Outcomes

<!-- Duplicated from index.qmd — keep in sync. -->

By the conclusion of this course, you will be able to:

1.  Identify meaningful gaps in a chosen field and translate them into well-scoped research problems.

2.  Formulate research questions that can be answered with data.

3.  Select and justify an appropriate quantitative method approach: description, statistical inference, predictive modeling, and/or causal reasoning.

4.  Use computational tools and AI to locate sources, operationalize concepts, analyze evidence, verify results, and document decisions responsibly.

5.  Design and defend a rigorous research approach.

6.  Interpret findings with appropriate uncertainty and limitations.

7.  Communicate results effectively in written and oral formats.

## How the Course Runs

The course meets **Monday, Wednesday, and Friday** in person, in 50-minute sessions, and each day of the week has a fixed job.

-   **Monday and Wednesday are flipped lectures led by a rotating [Student Research Lead](#the-student-research-lead) (SRL).** From Week 2 on, one of you runs each lecture as a **Socratic investigation**, not a slide summary: pose a puzzle, get the room to commit to an answer before opening any AI tool, direct the AI investigation, and defend a decision at the end. The instructor monitors for accuracy and formalizes the concept.

-   **Friday is a project studio.** No new topic content is introduced on Fridays. Each studio opens with a short **multiple-choice quiz** on the topic covered during the week, then runs a research **stand-up** and a **milestone sprint** kicked off from that week's Brightspace brief and worked with AI support.

### The Student Research Lead

Leading a lecture is a graded performance. Slots are randomly assigned at the beginning of the course, with no sequential assignment. You find your lead's SRL section in the notebook of the respective lecture. The recommendation is that you work on it one week ahead and submit a preparation script/notebook two days ahead, then run the room live.

## Course Materials

-   **Course book (free, required):** the course's own open text, [**EDR|AI** — **_Evidence-Driven Research in the Age of AI: How to Design, Analyze, Verify, and Defend_**](book/index.html){target="_blank"}, with AI generated translations in [Brazilian Portuguese](book-pt/index.html){target="_blank"} and [Spanish](book-es/index.html){target="_blank"}. It walks through the material at an undergraduate reading level, and every chapter has its **own companion Colab notebook** where you run the chapter's code and complete its closing **"It is your turn"** section. **EDR|AI is a work in progress**: it is still under development and will keep growing and improving during the semester.

-   **Theory text (free, recommended):** **Blair, Coppock & Humphreys (2023), *Research Design in the Social Sciences: Declaration, Diagnosis, and Redesign*** (RDSS, Princeton University Press) — read **free online** at [book.declaredesign.org](https://book.declaredesign.org/){target="_blank"}; no purchase required. The course book translates RDSS to the undergraduate audience, so each week the course-book chapters are **required** and the matching RDSS chapters are **recommended**.

-   **Optional companion:** Bergstrom & West, *Calling Bullshit* (public case studies at [callingbullshit.org](https://callingbullshit.org/){target="_blank"}), used lightly to sharpen claim evaluation. Any additional readings are posted on Brightspace.

-   **Computing (required):** A laptop or desktop with internet access and a modern web browser. Course activities run in the browser through [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/){target="_blank"}, with no local installation. There are **no purchases** required for this course.

-   **AI tools:** The course teaches responsible, documented AI use (see the [AI Policy](#ai-policy)). Approved tools:

    -   [**Google Gemini**](https://gemini.google.com/){target="_blank"} is the **primary** research assistant, used in and alongside Colab.
    -   [**Purdue GenAI Studio**](https://genai.rcac.purdue.edu){target="_blank"} supplies custom **reviewer roles** (for example, the Causal Identification Skeptic, the Poster Critic, and the Reproducibility Auditor) that you are encouraged to use when attacking your own work.
    -   [**Microsoft Copilot**](https://it.purdue.edu/newsroom/2024/240313-copilot-with-data-protection.php){target="_blank"} (Purdue-provided, with data protection) and other general-purpose AI tools are permitted **with disclosure**.

## Assessments

<!-- Weights come from course_config.yaml assessment: (v2, sums to 100). Keep the
     two in sync on every edit. -->

The course assesses the research chain itself: a semester-long research project carried through milestones, presented publicly at the Purdue Undergraduate Research Conference, and closed with a public evidence defense and a reproducible final research paper/chapter/note and AI-management portfolio.

| **Assessment component**                     | **Weight** |
|----------------------------------------------|-----------:|
| Attendance (iClicker; 85% target)            |         1% |
| Participation (rubric)                       |         9% |
| Quizzes                                      |        20% |
| Student Research Lead performance            |        20% |
| Final Project Milestones                     |        20% |
| Final Project                                |        20% |
| Research artifact (paper/chapter/note)       |        10% |

Attendance is checked with iClicker, with an 85% attendance target. The
Participation rubric incorporates lecture-notebook completion plus other
participation activities, such as feedback surveys and in-class exercises.
A recurring in-class activity is the **colleague audit**: each student
reviews the work of an instructor-created, AI-assisted simulated colleague
working a parallel project, using a fixed audit protocol and rubric; the
best 10 of 12 scored audits count within Participation. Every simulated
artifact is visibly marked as such, uses only real (never fabricated)
sources, and is debriefed in class the same session.

**Grading scale:** A ≥ 93, A− ≥ 90, B+ ≥ 87, B ≥ 83, B− ≥ 80, C+ ≥ 77, C ≥ 73, C− ≥ 70, D ≥ 60, F < 60 (no curve).

Additional information about Purdue undergraduate research conferences: <https://www.purdue.edu/undergrad-research/conferences/index.php>{target="_blank"}.

### Grade Challenges

Students who wish to challenge a grade must do so **within 3 calendar days** of the grade's release. An exception applies for the last week of class, when assignments must be challenged **within 1 calendar day** to ensure timely computation of final course grades. Grade challenges must be grounded in legitimate disputes over research-methods principles or grading accuracy. Challenges based on post-hoc legalistic arguments or subjective dissatisfaction will not be considered.

To challenge an assignment score:

1.  **Review posted solutions / rubrics** thoroughly.
2.  If you still believe an error has been made, email the instructor with:
    -   Course name, section, and date/time
    -   Your name and Student ID
    -   Assignment number / title
    -   Specific deduction being challenged
    -   Reason for the challenge, with reference to the solutions or grading rubric

> *Grades will not be discussed in class — before, during, or after class. Please use office hours for questions related to course content or assignment clarification. After the challenge period, all grades are final and cannot be revised further for purposes of calculating final course grades.*

## Course Policies and Additional Details

### AI Policy

This course explicitly teaches **responsible, documented AI use**. You are expected to use AI at high intensity, under tight control, and always as **your arm and your research assistant, not your brain**.

**The discipline.** Every use of AI in this course follows the full workflow **Specify, Delegate, Interrogate, Inspect, Verify, Document, Defend** (the everyday shorthand is **Ask, Verify, Document**). You specify the task precisely, delegate it to the tool, interrogate and inspect what comes back, verify it against real evidence, document what you decided, and defend the result as your own.

**The AI Research Ledger.** Every deliverable and every notebook session appends an entry to your **AI Research Ledger**, with eight fields: **task delegated, tool used, prompt, output summary, decision, verification method, remaining concern, and responsible researcher**. A missing ledger entry returns the submission.

**Verify everything.** AI tools routinely fabricate citations, sources, and facts. Every claim and every source you submit must be independently located and confirmed to exist and to say what you claim it says. Any errors or omissions from your use of an AI tool are your responsibility. **Undisclosed or unverified AI output is an academic-integrity violation.**

**What is yours alone.** Some decisions are never delegated to an AI tool. You, and only you, are responsible for:

-   selecting the research problem and question;
-   declaring the research design and target population;
-   choosing measurements and evaluating data quality;
-   ethical judgments;
-   deciding which claims the evidence justifies;
-   acknowledging uncertainty and limitations;
-   defending the project publicly.

**Approved tools.** Google Gemini is the primary in-notebook research assistant. Purdue GenAI Studio supplies reviewer roles you must consult at four milestones (M5, M7, M9, M13). Microsoft Copilot and other general-purpose tools are permitted with disclosure. You are **not permitted to use AI tools during any closed assessment** where its use is prohibited. Low-effort prompts produce low-quality output; refine your prompts using the course concepts.
